raw_response.country: Multiple countries globally (257 studies: 46% Asia, 40% Africa, 4% Latin America/Caribbean, 4% North America, 2% Oceania, 1% Europe, 4% multiple regions)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household, community, school, and public water and sanitation service access and conditions across 257 empirical studies (115 water, 57 sanitation, 85 both).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain reading (yes): one of the review's three core conceptual and coding domains is 'Institutional Structures' (173 articles), including '3.a Formal Laws & Policies' (21 articles) as well as community WASH governance and water user committees under 'Decision-making' and 'Leadership'. Narrow 2026-10-13 reading (no): the review's analytic focus is women's and girls' empowerment (agency, bodily integrity, personal/household resources, and gender norms/relations) rather than legal or administrative rule-type mechanisms directly governing WASH service access. In Section 3.a, the synthesis primarily addresses gender quotas and women's representation/voice on community WASH committees, barriers to female WASH entrepreneurship, and watershed project participation (generic community project governance and empowerment outcomes rather than service-access rules). Isolated one-sentence descriptive references to intra-household/personal land ownership, difficulties obtaining toilet subsidies, pay-per-use public toilet costs, school sex-segregated toilet mandates, or public toilet maintenance guidelines summarize individual cited studies under empowerment/resource themes without analyzing any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing household or community service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Systematic empirical synthesis: a PRISMA-reported systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis using best-fit framework synthesis and MMAT appraisal of 257 peer-reviewed empirical studies (129 qualitative, 54 quantitative, 74 mixed-methods).
criterion_notes.c4: Although primarily synthesizing empowerment subdomains (health, safety/violence, privacy, time, agency), the review also reports outcomes relevant to household latrine/improved sanitation ownership, water source selection and quantity, public toilet affordability, maintenance of public sanitary complexes, and caste- or movement-based exclusion from water and sanitation facilities.
criterion_notes.c5: Study design (systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis), study populations and units of analysis (individual women and girls and households across 257 studies, ~1,600,348 participants), and bidirectional WASH and empowerment constructs are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This review a) identified empirical water and sanitation research that engaged empowerment and/or empowerment-related domains; b) reported empowerment-related terminology used, research locations, methods leveraged, if water and/or sanitation was the focus; and c) synthesized evidence.

Any peer-reviewed article presenting primary or secondary research related to water and/or sanitation and either empowerment and/or one of the domains of empowerment from the conceptual model was eligible for inclusion.

Women’s participation in WASH-related governance has been constrained by a lack of awareness about the rules (Uganda [102]), a lack of transparency or distrust in political institutions (Kenya [87]), husbands or sons attending meetings in their place (India [106]), and being ignored by men (Kenya [61]).

WASH policies, and uneven policy awareness, implementation, and enforcement, have posed barriers to women. Female entrepreneurs in Cambodia found certain policies made it hard to run water enterprises [30]. Even when policies exist to address women’s and girls’ needs, they are not always known or enforced.

With respect to sanitation, in India, the odds of having a latrine was significantly higher in households where women were the main decision makers [136] and in Kenya, the likelihood of a household owning an improved sanitation facility was significantly higher when women had at least some input on decisions about major household purchases [134].
Limited household income has forced women to prioritize needs like food over sanitation, whether investing in or paying to use toilets [135, 147, 186].

raw_response.exposure: Bidirectional water and sanitation conditions, behaviors, and WASH programs/initiatives in relation to domains of women's and girls' empowerment (agency, resources, and institutional structures including gender norms, interpersonal relations, and community governance participation)
raw_response.outcome: Women's and girls' empowerment domains (decision-making, leadership, collective action, freedom of movement, bodily integrity/safety/health/privacy, critical consciousness, financial/productive assets, knowledge/skills, social capital, time, and institutional norms/relations) and associated household/community water and sanitation access, latrine ownership, affordability, and use
raw_response.population_and_sample: Estimated 1,600,348 participants across 257 peer-reviewed empirical studies (129 qualitative, 54 quantitative, 74 mixed-methods) focusing on women and girls (40% female-only samples, 54% male and female samples, 5% unspecified; 69% adults, 5% adolescents, 22% multiple populations)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification of Criterion 2. This systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis of 257 empirical WASH studies examines the bidirectional relationship between water/sanitation conditions or programs and women's and girls' empowerment (agency, bodily integrity/resources, and social norms/relations). Although it passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 via its 'Institutional Structures' / 'Formal Laws & Policies' coding domain and community WASH governance themes (plain_criterion2_decision: 'include'), Section 3.a predominantly examines gender quotas and women's representation/voice on community water committees, barriers to female water entrepreneurship, and watershed participation rather than rules governing household or community service access, while isolated single-sentence mentions of personal land ownership, subsidy difficulties, pay-per-use toilet fees, school toilet mandates, or public sanitary complex maintenance summarize individual cited studies under broad empowerment/resource themes rather than analyzing a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis (best-fit framework synthesis of 257 empirical studies: 129 qualitative, 54 quantitative, and 74 mixed-methods)
